statements.quote: This study was pre-registered at Open Science Framework, and all data are available at: https://osf.io/h6ztr/

Based on this research, we pre-registered this hypothesis: Hypothesis 1. Individuals who received AI assistance will produce ideas of higher quantity and quality, but lower flexibility than individuals working alone.

We pre-registered this hypothesis: Hypothesis 2. Individuals anticipating a human teammate will produce ideas of higher quantity, quality, and flexibility compared to those anticipating an AI teammate.
statements.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2 (The Collective Effort Model), Hypothesis 2

statements.quote: We have these non-preregistered hypotheses that: Hypothesis 3a. Idea quantity and quality will be highest when individuals receive AI assistance and anticipate a human teammate (AI-HHT), followed by no-AI assistance and anticipate a human teammate (HHT), followed by no-AI assistance with an anticipated AI teammate (HAT), and lowest when individuals receive AI assistance with an anticipated AI teammate (AI-HAT).
statements.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2, introduction to non-preregistered Hypotheses 3a and 3b; excerpt through Hypothesis 3a

statements.quote: Hypothesis 3b. Idea flexibility will be highest when individuals do not receive AI assistance and anticipate a human teammate (HHT), followed by AI-assisted ideation with an anticipated human teammate (AI-HHT), followed by no-AI assistance with an anticipated AI teammate (HAT), and lowest when individuals receive AI assistance with an anticipated AI teammate (AI-HAT).
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation and were acknowledged that their responses would remain confidential and used only for research purposes.

Microsoft Co-pilot was selected for two primary reasons. First, as a university-licensed platform, it meets institutional data-security and privacy standards, ensuring the protection and confidentially of participants' responses. Second, each participant accessed the system through an individual account, which reduced shared-account use and minimized the potential for cross-participant data contamination or AI self-learning effects that could arise from repeated interactions through a single account.
statements.locator: pp. 4-5, Section 4.2 (Study design), data security and accounts

statements.quote: Before beginning the task, participants received standardized instructions explaining that Co-Pilot should be treated as an assisting tool for asking specific questions or getting suggestions, rather than using AI-generated responses verbatim. Participants had to type out their ideas and could not use AI-generated responses verbatim.

After the completion of the brainstorming task, participants completed a post-study questionnaire that included a manipulation check of impression management and measurements regarding one's motivation to engage in the task.

After obtaining informed consent, participants watched a brief 2-min video demonstrating traditional group brainstorming techniques developed by IDEO. The researcher then emphasized the four core rules of brainstorming, which are deferring judgment, encouraging wild ideas, needing the quantity of ideas, and building on each other's ideas (Osborn, 1953), and provided a printed copy for reference throughout the session.
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 4.3 (Procedure), video and printed materials

statements.quote: After the video, participants were then presented with the main brainstorming task: “Student Orientation, Advising, and Registration (SOAR) is a specific program designed to transition incoming students as a new “Badger". You are a member of SOAR planning team! Recently, however, SOAR has received several complaints from students that SOAR is not fun, so your job is to improve or redesign this program to make it more engaging and helpful for future students. The goal is to ensure that the future Badgers have a smooth and enjoyable transition into their university life.”

Participants in the AI-assisted condition were instructed to use Microsoft Co-Pilot as an assisting tool by asking “what” and “how” questions to generate ideas. Each participant logged into their university-licensed Co-Pilot account, and researchers provided step-by-step instructions. The research team assured participants that all interactions would remain confidential and that AI chat histories would be deleted immediately after data collection to ensure privacy.
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 4.3 (Procedure), AI instructions and chat histories

statements.quote: Quantity of ideas. The total number of unique ideas typed by participants in the Word document was taken as quantity of ideas.

Quality of ideas. Trained undergraduate coders, blind to condition, used a coding scheme to rate ideas. Ideas were assessed on three dimensions: 1). originality, representing the novelty and uniqueness of the idea; 2). feasibility, referring to the ease of implementation of the idea; 3). fun, representing the perceived enjoyability of the idea. Each coder rated each dimension on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). A mean score was calculated for each participant by averaging their ratings across all generated ideas. Because data were collected in two semesters, coding was conducted in two corresponding periods. During the first period, four trained coders jointly coded approximately 16% of the ideas to establish interrater reliability. The interclass correlation coefficient (ICCs) were .76 for originality, .70 for feasibility, and .71 for fun, all exceeding the commonly accepted .70 threshold, indicating strong reliability across the three quality dimensions. During the second coding period, one coder was replaced due to scheduling constraints. To re-establish reliability, the new coder and the continuing coder independently coded approximately 20% of the ideas, yielding acceptable intercoder reliability with ICCs = .84, .78, and .75 respectively for originality, feasibility, and fun. Additionally, the averaged ratings from those jointly coded subsets served as the final scores for those ideas. After reliability was confirmed for each period, the remaining ideas were randomly distributed among the coders, who independently rated them using a blind-coding procedure.
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 4.4 (Measures), coding scheme, participant scores, and two periods of data coding

statements.quote: Flexibility of ideas. Idea flexibility was assessed by counting the number of distinct idea categories produced by each participant, reflecting the diversity of their idea pool. The categorization scheme was developed collaboratively through an in-depth discussion involving the research team and trained coders. The team first generated preliminary notes on recurring idea types, then through discussion, refined these observations into a comprehensive set of thirteen mutually exclusive categories that captured the full range of responses without imposing overly narrow distinctions. For example, although activities such as going on a picnic, playing bingo, participating in icebreaker games, or hosting a flea market represent different specific suggestions, they were all classified under the broader category of social activities. After the coding scheme was finalized, trained coders jointly coded ideas from 15 participants to establish consistency, so any discrepancies were discussed and resolved through consensus. Following this in-depth discussion, the coders were randomly assigned an equivalent number of participants and independently coded participants’ ideas according to the established coding scheme, while remaining blind to the experimental condition. The flexibility score for each participant was calculated as the total number of unique categories represented in their idea list.

Impression management. Participants' perception of their impression management during the task was measured using eleven items adapted from Wayne and Ferris (1990). All items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale (from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). Because participants anticipated to interact with either a human or an AI partner, item wording was adjusted slightly by replacing “partner” with “AI partner” in the AI condition. Although eleven items were included in the full questionnaire, six of them focused specifically on behaviors occurring during or after the interaction with the partner. Because the present study aimed to assess impression management during the individual idea generation phase, five items most appropriate for capturing pre-interaction impression management were used for this study. These items include, “do you present your partner as a friendly and approachable person?“, “do you let your partner know you are committed to doing a good job?“, “do you work harder because you will be evaluated by your partner?“, “do you make your partner aware of your contribution to the team's effort?“, and “do you make sure your partner sees you as responsible for team's positive outcomes?“. Responses on these five items were averaged to present participants' impression management score during the individual idea generation phase (Cronbach's alpha = .75).
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 4.4 (Measures), questionnaire items and scoring

statements.quote: Demographics. Participants reported their age, gender, ethnicity, race, and academic major. Residency status was also collected to ensure accurate distribution of monetary rewards.

Participants’ responses were collected in individual documents and subsequently coded to generate quantitative indicators of idea performance. Creative performance was operationalized along multiple dimensions, including idea quantity, quality, and flexibility. Trained coders evaluated all responses using predefined coding criteria. Inter-coder reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), indicating acceptable levels of agreement. Idea flexibility was assessed through a categorization approach based on a predefined coding scheme developed through iterative coder discussion. To test the hypotheses, analyses of variance (ANOVA) were conducted. Where significant interaction effects were identified, follow-up simple effects were examined using pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means with Bonferroni adjustment. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software version 27.
statements.locator: p. 6, Section 4.5 (Data analysis), source documents, coding, and software

statements.quote: Contrary to our pre-registered Hypothesis 1, AI assistance was associated with lower idea quantity compared to independent brainstorming.
statements.locator: p. 6, Section 5.2 (Quantity of ideas), preregistration reference

statements.quote: This supports the quality component of our pre-registered Hypothesis 1, specifically with respect to idea originality.
statements.locator: p. 6, Section 5.3 (Quality of idea), Originality, preregistration reference

statements.quote: This suggests that participants anticipating a human partner outperformed those anticipating collaboration with an AI teammate, supporting our pre-registered Hypothesis 2 that anticipating a human partner led to higher idea quality.
This supports the quality component of our pre-registered Hypothesis 1, especially the enjoyableness of ideas.
This supports our pre-registered Hypothesis 2 that anticipating a human partner led to higher idea quality.
This supports the flexibility component our pre-registered Hypothesis 1.
statements.locator: p. 7, Section 5.4 (Flexibility of idea), preregistration reference

statements.quote: Participants who received AI assistance produced ideas that were significantly more original and enjoyable than those who worked independently, yet their ideas exhibited lower flexibility (in support of pre-registered Hypothesis 1).
statements.locator: p. 7, Section 6.1 (Influence of AI assistance), preregistration reference

notes:
Checked 2026-10-09. Read all 77095 characters of the supplied markdown in six contiguous chunks, including the Appendix and references; checked relevant passages against the 10-page PDF with PyMuPDF. Quotes are copied from PDF text with layout line breaks and discretionary line-end hyphenation normalized. The only data/preregistration URL in the paper is https://osf.io/h6ztr/; the form has the same data_url and an empty code_url. No external supplementary-material or code-repository link is stated. The Appendix's Fig. 1 and Tables 1-2 are part of the article, not a separate data deposit.

Two relevant public OSF records were inspected, both containing only the same blank questionnaire, plus public preregistration text in h6ztr. Neither provides actual participant IDs, assignments, outcome scores, or participant texts/ideas. Thus no public participant-level data were confirmed despite the paper's 'all data are available' claim. This is materials-only availability, not an on-request or restricted dataset. The conclusion concerns contents accessible at the checked records; it is not proof that no data exist elsewhere.

No per-person or per-arm means, SDs, SEs, analyzed counts, exclusion counts, or diversity measures can be recomputed from the available materials. what_we_could_compute is null because no public observations were available. rows_checked and columns_checked are null because the only files are survey instruments, not data tables.

final.open_items item 5 can be clarified from the preregistration (a protocol finding, not a computable statistic): at https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/h6ztr/, attributes.registration_responses['q15.question'] states:
We focus on three primary outcome variables:
Quantity of ideas — the total number of ideas generated by each participant or team.
Quality of ideas — assessed on three dimensions:
- Originality (novelty and uniqueness),
- Feasibility (ease of implementation),
- Fun (level of enjoyment or creativity appeal).
Flexibility of ideas — measured by the diversity of idea categories represented.
This names quantity, quality, and flexibility as primary outcome families, with originality, feasibility, and fun within quality; no single primary endpoint is selected.

For final.open_items 1-2, preregistration q14.question states:
Phase 1 (Ideation Condition). In the first phase, we manipulated the ideation condition. Participants were randomly assigned to either (a) generate ideas independently or (b) generate ideas with assistance from an AI.
Phase 2 (Teaming Condition). In the second phase, we manipulated the teaming condition. Participants were then paired with either (a) a human teammate or (b) an AI teammate to collaboratively brainstorm and select ideas.
This supports intended random assignment of AI assistance but does not supply an implemented randomization protocol, session/pair identifiers, or allocation records that resolve the actual assignment mechanism or clustering. Items 3-4 remain unresolved: no assignment/exclusion records and no original SPSS syntax/output were found. Preregistration q17.question specifies two-way ANOVA but does not settle the reported eta-squared label or marginal-means issue.

Searches covered full article title and first author in DataCite, Zenodo, Harvard Dataverse, and OSF, plus the different registered-project title and the first author's public OSF projects/registrations. All successful result sets were reviewed; relevant duplicates are not counted as separate deposits. Failed Zenodo size=100 calls are recorded with null counts; anonymous size=25 retries succeeded. No GitHub repository was named, so no GitHub API calls were used.

Publisher limitation: the DOI returned an Elsevier forwarding page (HTTP 200); the ScienceDirect article page returned HTTP 403 and was not bypassed, so unlinked publisher supplements could not be ruled out. Confidence is high in the materials-only classification of the verified OSF records, with this publisher limitation on broader completeness. No login, account creation, access request, or saved data download was used.
